kl-01.title: Korean Language and Literature: Learning to Read Language and Literature
explain: The discipline that looks closely at the language we speak and the writing made in that language is **Korean language and literature** (국어국문학). It divides broadly into two branches. One examines language itself: **Korean linguistics** (국어학). The other examines works built out of language: **Korean literary studies** (국문학, the study of literature).

Here "국어" (literally "national language") is the name Koreans use for their own language, while the name used from outside is "한국어" (Korean). The word "국어" survives in the name of the discipline. "한글" (Hangul) is the name not of a language but of a **script**. The language is Korean, and the script that writes it is Hangul. Korean existed even in the era before Hangul was known.

**Korean linguistics** asks how language is put together. It looks at which sounds are used (phonemes), how words are made (words), how words connect to form sentences (sentences), how meaning is conveyed, and how the language has changed over time.

**Korean literary studies** asks how a work was made and what it makes us feel. It distinguishes genres such as poetry, fiction, and drama, reads the characters and voices within a single work, and compares works from the same period or the same genre. It covers everything from old works to today's.

explain.alt: A diagram of stacked units of language. From bottom to top: phoneme (the smallest sound that distinguishes meaning, e.g. the sounds m, u, l), word (a unit with meaning, e.g. the word for 'water'), sentence (a thought expressed as one unit, e.g. 'the water is clear'), and text (a body formed by gathered sentences, e.g. a poem, a story, a letter), linked by an upward arrow.
explain.caption: The units of language stack from smallest to largest.

explain: The two branches are connected. A poem is writing that uses the sound and meaning of language with great precision, so reading poetry requires knowing how language is structured. Conversely, how language is actually used shows itself vividly in literary works. This course sequence moves from sounds and letters, through words and sentences, to reading poems and stories.

examples.title: Looking at the same sentence with two eyes
body: Suppose there is a sentence "비가 그쳤다" ("The rain has stopped"). Seen through the eyes of Korean linguistics, "비" (rain) is a word that refers to a thing, "그쳤다" (stopped) expresses an action, and "가" sets "비" up as the subject of the sentence. In terms of sound, it is a chain of phonemes such as ㅂ and ㅣ.

Seen through the eyes of literary studies, what matters is what this sentence makes us feel when it is placed on the first line of a poem. Whether it is relief or emptiness depends on the lines that follow. Even the same sentence prompts different questions.

kl-02.title: Sounds and Hangul: The Principles of Hunminjeongeum
explain: Hangul is a script whose creator, date, and principles are known with relative clarity. King Sejong of Joseon created it in 1443 and announced it to the world (promulgation) in 1446 under the name "훈민정음" (Hunminjeongeum). Hunminjeongeum means "the correct sounds for instructing the people." Along with the letters themselves, a book explaining the principles behind them (the Hunminjeongeum Haerye, or explanatory edition) was also used at that time.

A **consonant** is a sound produced when the flow of air is blocked or narrowed somewhere in the mouth, while a **vowel** is a sound produced by resonance in the mouth without such obstruction. Hunminjeongeum created the two types on different principles.

For consonants, five letters were first made by imitating the **shape of the speech organs** as the sound is produced. These are called the basic letters. ㄱ is the shape of the root of the tongue blocking the throat, ㄴ is the shape of the tongue touching the upper gum ridge, ㅁ is the shape of the mouth, ㅅ is the shape of a tooth, and ㅇ is the shape of the throat.

The remaining consonants were made by **adding strokes** to the basic letters. Strokes were added as the sound grows stronger. From ㄴ came ㄷ, and from ㄷ came ㅌ; from ㅁ came ㅂ, and from ㅂ came ㅍ. From the shape of the letters alone one can tell that they form a group of closely related sounds.

explain.alt: A diagram showing the five basic consonant letters and the letters made by adding strokes. The top row has the basic letters for g (shape of the tongue root blocking the throat), n (shape of the tongue touching the upper gum ridge), m (shape of the mouth), s (shape of a tooth), and the silent-initial ng letter (shape of the throat). The bottom row shows the letters made by adding strokes: g→k, n→d→t, m→b→p, s→j→ch, and the silent letter→h.
explain.caption: Consonants: five basic letters and the letters formed by adding strokes.

explain: For **vowels**, three basic letters were made by imitating heaven, earth, and humans. Heaven is a round dot (ㆍ), earth is a flat line (ㅡ), and humans are a standing line (ㅣ). Combining these produces the other vowels. A dot above ㅡ gives ㅗ, a dot to the right of ㅣ gives ㅏ, a dot below ㅡ gives ㅜ, and a dot to the left of ㅣ gives ㅓ. The dot (ㆍ) is a letter no longer used today, but it remains at the basis of the shapes of the vowels.

explain.alt: A vowel diagram. The top row states that the round dot is heaven, the flat horizontal line is earth, and the vertical line is humans. The bottom row states that the vowel o is a dot above the horizontal line, a is a dot to the right of the vertical line, u is a dot below the horizontal line, and eo is a dot to the left of the vertical line.
explain.caption: The basic vowel letters and the four letters made by combining them.

explain: Because the shape of the letters is connected to the nature of the sounds in this way, Hangul is often called a "scientific script." This means that, rather than memorizing new letters, once you know the principle, the rest follows by understanding.

ㄴ, ㄷ, and ㅌ follow the same principle. ㄴ is the shape of the tongue touching the upper gum ridge, and each time a stroke is added the sound grows stronger.

kl-03.title: Words and Sentences: Parts of Speech and Sentence Components
explain:
Within a single sentence, words do different jobs. The categories into which words are divided according to their function and form are called **parts of speech** (품사). School grammar commonly divides them into nine.
- **Noun** (명사): the name of a person or thing (아이 'child', 책 'book')
- **Pronoun** (대명사): refers in place of a name (나 'I', 그것 'that')
- **Numeral** (수사): expresses number (하나 'one', 둘째 'second')
- **Verb** (동사): action (읽다 'to read', 가다 'to go')
- **Adjective** (형용사): state or quality (예쁘다 'to be pretty', 작다 'to be small')
- **Determiner** (관형사): modifies a noun (새 'new', 헌 'old')
- **Adverb** (부사): mainly modifies verbs and adjectives (빨리 'quickly', 매우 'very')
- **Particle** (조사): attaches after a word to express a relation (이/가, 을/를)
- **Interjection** (감탄사): expresses a feeling or a call (아 'ah', 어머 'oh my')

The way of dividing parts of speech differs from scholar to scholar. Here we use the nine parts of speech most commonly taught in school. A feature of Korean is that a **particle** is a separate word. "아이가" is seen as two words, "아이" and "가", yet in spacing they are written together. The unit of spacing is called an **eojeol** (어절, a spacing unit).

Verbs and adjectives are easy to confuse. There is an easy way to tell them apart. If attaching "-는다/-ㄴ다" (the plain present-tense ending) sounds natural, it is a verb; if it sounds awkward, it is an adjective. "먹는다" is natural, but "예쁜다" is awkward. So 먹다 ('to eat') is a verb and 예쁘다 ('to be pretty') is an adjective.

Now let us look at the positions words take within a sentence. These are called **sentence components** (문장 성분).
- **Main components**: the skeleton of the sentence. Subject (who), predicate (does what), object (what), and complement (the word before 되다 'become' or 아니다 'be not')
- **Subordinate components**: modify the skeleton. Adnominal (modifies a noun) and adverbial (mainly modifies the predicate)
- **Independent component**: the interjection phrase, which stands apart from the rest of the sentence (the "아" in "아, 비가 온다", 'Ah, it's raining')

explain.alt: A diagram dividing the Korean sentence meaning 'The small child reads a book in the library' into five boxes. 'Small' is labeled adnominal, 'the child' (with subject particle) subject, 'in the library' adverbial, 'the book' (with object particle) object, and 'reads' predicate. The boxes for the child, the book, and reads have green borders, while those for small and in the library have gray borders. Below, it states that green means main components and gray means subordinate components, and that 'small' modifies the child and 'in the library' modifies reads.
explain.caption: The names of the sentence components.

explain: Because the subject and predicate are the skeleton, a sentence cannot stand without these two. By contrast, a sentence still holds without the adnominal and the adverbial. Even if "작은" and "도서관에서" are removed from the sentence in the diagram, "아이가 책을 읽는다" ('The child reads a book') remains.

examples.title: Breaking a sentence into components
body: Dividing "작은 아이가 도서관에서 책을 읽는다" into eojeol gives five chunks. 아이가 is the subject, 책을 is the object, and 읽는다 is the predicate, and these three are the skeleton. To these are attached "작은", an adnominal modifying 아이, and "도서관에서", an adverbial telling the place of reading.
A modifier usually stands right before the word it modifies. "작은" modifies "아이가", and "도서관에서" modifies "읽는다".

kl-04.title: Literary Genres: Lyric, Narrative, Drama, Didactic
explain: Literary works can be divided into several genres according to their purpose and the way they are made. This is because comparing works of the same genre makes the characteristics of each work easier to see. The division commonly used in Korean class is the four genres of **lyric (서정), narrative (서사), drama (극), and didactic (교술)**. There is also a method that divides literature into only three genres, lyric, narrative, and drama, so the classification may differ depending on whose division of which scholar is followed. Here we take the four-genre view.

**Lyric** is the genre that sings of the feelings and thoughts of a person who faces the world. It is short, and often refines the sound and imagery of language with great care. Poetry (시) and sijo (시조, a short traditional Korean verse form) are representative.
**Narrative** is the genre that conveys events as a story. There are characters, and events follow one another. Traditional tales (설화, folktales) and novels belong here.
**Drama** is the genre in which characters speak and act directly on stage to show the story. It is writing meant to be read and also writing meant to be performed. It includes plays and screenplays.
**Didactic** writing is the genre that aims to inform and teach experience, thoughts, and knowledge. The writer steps forward and speaks directly. Essays, diaries, and letters belong here.

explain.alt: A diagram showing the four literary genres in four boxes. Lyric sings one's own feelings (e.g. poetry, sijo), narrative tells events (e.g. novels, folktales), drama shows on stage (e.g. plays, screenplays), and didactic informs and teaches (e.g. essays, diaries). Below, it states that a single work may also carry the qualities of two genres together.
explain.caption: The four literary genres and examples.

explain: The reason for dividing genres is not to attach labels to works. Knowing which genre a work belongs to lets us decide what to watch for when reading. For lyric, we look at the speaker's voice; for narrative, the flow of events; for drama, the dialogue and action. Many works lie on the borders, and two genres may mix, as in a poem written in prose or a song that holds a story.

examples.title: Genre determines how to read
body: "Yesterday on the way to school I met a cat. At first I was startled, but soon I grew fond of it." Writing like this, in which the writer directly informs us of her own experience, is closer to didactic.

"The cat jumped over the wall. The child chased after it." This writing takes on the quality of narrative because what the characters do follows in sequence. And writing that bursts out a feeling, like "Ah, those small footprints beyond the wall!", takes on the quality of lyric.

kl-05.title: Reading Poetry: Speaker, Tone, Imagery, Figurative Language
explain: Let us learn the basic tools for reading poetry, the representative lyric genre. In this lesson we practice on a short poem written for the purpose.

The alley after the rain
The wet wall cools slowly.
I fold my umbrella
and call your name, once.
My heart is an empty teacup,
still warm.

First, the **speaker**. The speaker is the person who talks within the poem. In the poem above, "I" is the speaker. The speaker is sometimes the same as the person who wrote the poem (the poet), but we cannot assume so, because it may be a voice the poet has created. So it is safer to write "the speaker says this" than "the poet felt this."

**Tone** is the atmosphere given off by the speaker's manner of speaking and attitude. The tone of the poem above is calm without any loud voice, a little lonely, and leaning toward longing for someone. Tone is read from word choice, sentence endings, and scenes quietly piled up.

**Imagery** is the sensory picture that rises in the mind when reading a poem. There is the visual, as if seen with the eyes (the wet wall); the auditory, felt through sound; the olfactory, of smell; the gustatory, of taste; and the tactile, felt on the skin (still warm). Imagery makes a scene concrete and thereby conveys feeling.

**Figurative language** is a way of speaking of one thing by comparing it to another. The thing being compared is called the **tenor** (원관념), and the thing it is compared to is called the **vehicle** (보조관념). Saying directly that things are alike by using words like "as" or "like" is a **simile** (직유), and saying "A is B" without such words is a **metaphor** (은유).

explain.alt: A diagram showing a metaphor. The left box is the tenor "my heart," the right box is the vehicle "an empty teacup," and the two boxes are joined by a line labeled "compared to." A box below gives their shared point as "being empty, yet warmth remains." At the very bottom it states that a simile is a way of comparing using words such as "as" or "like."
explain.caption: The structure of a metaphor: tenor, vehicle, and shared point.

explain: In the poem above, "My heart is an empty teacup" is a metaphor. The tenor is "my heart," and the vehicle is "an empty teacup." The shared points are that it is empty, and yet some warmth still remains. If the same statement is written as "My heart is like an empty teacup," it becomes a simile.

examples.title: The order for reading a poem
body:
1. Find who is speaking (speaker).
2. Pick out the manner of speech and the atmosphere (tone).
3. Find the scenes that can be seen or felt in the body (imagery).
4. Find what is compared to what, and state the shared point (figurative language).

"The wet wall cools slowly" is a scene mixing the visual and the tactile, and it makes us feel the unhurried time after the rain has stopped. This scene connects with the "empty teacup" that follows, and the two gather into a single feeling: warmth remaining within loneliness.

kl-06.title: Reading and Writing Stories: Character, Event, Setting, Point of View
explain: The basics of reading the narrative genre are three: **character** (who), **event** (what happens), and **setting** (when and where). These three form the skeleton of a story. To them is added **point of view** (시점), which concerns who tells the story.
First, let us read a very short story written for this purpose.

On the morning she moved out, Mina left the key on the windowsill of the empty room. Before closing the door, she looked back one more time. On the wall remained the pencil marks that had measured her height. Mina ran her hand over the marks once, and closed the door.

The **character** is Mina. Her personality shows through her outward actions alone. The **event** is leaving the room on moving day, and the act of running her hand over the pencil marks is the center of the event. The **setting** is the empty room on the morning of moving day. Setting also creates the mood of a story. The empty room gives off loneliness and a sense of ending.

**Point of view** is who tells the story and from where. The narrator (서술자) is the voice that tells the story. The story above shows only Mina's actions from outside the story, and does not directly say what Mina is thinking. This is the third-person observer point of view.

First-person protagonist: the protagonist inside the story, who knows his or her own inner thoughts. First-person observer: inside the story, watching from the side, who knows only outward appearances. Third-person observer: outside the story, who knows only outward appearances. Omniscient author: outside the story, who knows the inner thoughts of all characters. Below, it states that the narrator is the voice that tells the story.

explain: Even the same scene changes when the point of view changes. Writing "I left the key on the windowsill, and the pencil marks on the wall lingered long in my eyes" gives a first-person protagonist point of view, in which I can speak my own inner thoughts directly. Writing "Mina recalled the five years she had spent here, and her heart was heavy" gives an omniscient author point of view, which knows inner thoughts.

"My sister left the key on the windowsill. I could not tell what she was thinking, but she stroked the pencil marks on the wall for a long time." The younger sister does not know her sister's inner thoughts and speaks only of outward appearances.
When the point of view changes, what the reader knows and does not know changes. The reader comes to fill the unknown parts with imagination. This is one of the pleasures of reading a story.

kl-07.title: The Four Types of Korean Phonological Alternation and Multi-Step Derivation
explain: The phenomenon in which the phonemes of the underlying form change depending on the environment when morphemes combine and are realized as actual pronunciation (the surface form) is called **phonological alternation** (음운 변동). Korean phonological alternations are classified into four types according to the number of phonemes and the manner of change: **substitution** (교체, A → B), **deletion** (탈락, AB → A), **insertion** (첨가, A → AB), and **coalescence** (축약, AB → C).

**Substitution** is a phenomenon in which one phoneme changes into another, so that the total number of phonemes is maintained. It includes the **syllable-final neutralization rule** (음절 끝소리 규칙, neutralization to unreleased stops), in which the final consonant is pronounced as only seven sounds, 'ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅇ'; **nasalization** (비음화), in which a stop changes into a nasal before a nasal ('국물' 'soup' → [궁물]); **lateralization** (유음화), in which 'ㄴ' and 'ㄹ' meet and assimilate to 'ㄹ' ('신라' 'Silla' → [실라]); **palatalization** (구개음화), in which 'ㄷ, ㅌ' change into 'ㅈ, ㅊ' before the grammatical morpheme '이' ('굳이' 'obstinately' → [구지]); and **tensification** (된소리되기, fortition).

explain.alt: A diagram comparing the four types of Korean phonological alternation (substitution, deletion, insertion, coalescence) and the multi-step derivation of /읊고/→[읍꼬] and /놓다/→[노타]
explain.caption: The change in the total number of phonemes differs according to the type of phonological alternation.

explain: **Deletion** is a phenomenon in which one of two phonemes disappears so that the number of phonemes decreases by one. Representative cases are **consonant cluster simplification** (자음군 단순화), in which only one of a double final consonant remains ('닭' 'chicken' → [닥]), deletion of 'ㅎ' between vowels ('좋아' 'is good' → [조아]), and deletion of stem-final 'ㅡ' ('쓰어' → [써]). **Insertion** is a phenomenon in which a new phoneme that was not there intervenes; an example is **n-insertion** (ㄴ 첨가), which occurs at the boundary of a compound or derived word when the first element ends in a consonant and the second begins with '이, 야, 여, 요, 유' ('솜이불' 'cotton quilt' → [솜니불]). **Coalescence** is a phenomenon in which two phonemes combine to become a single third phoneme; an example is **aspiration** (거센소리되기), in which 'ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅈ' meet 'ㅎ' and become an aspirated sound ('놓다' 'to put down' → [노타]), which reduces the number of phonemes by one.

When several rules apply in sequence to a single word, the **order of rule application** (feeding and bleeding relations) is important. For example, for `/읊고/`, consonant cluster simplification (deletion, ㄿ→ㅂ) occurs first to give `/읍고/`, and then tensification after a stop (substitution) applies to give `[읍꼬]`. Also, `/물약/` ('liquid medicine') becomes `/물냑/` by n-insertion, and then, through lateralization (substitution), is derived as `[물략]`.

There are limits and exceptions to note. Palatalization does not occur in compound words where lexical morphemes follow one another ('밭이랑' [반니랑], 'furrow of a field'), and occurs only before **grammatical morphemes** (형식형태소) such as particles or suffixes ('같이' 'together' [가치]). Also, '밟다' [밥따] and '넓죽하다' [넙쭈카다] are exceptions to the general rule for verb stems in consonant cluster simplification, where 'ㄹ' remains, and 'ㅂ' remains instead.

examples.title: Comparing the change in the number of phonemes in /국민/ and /국화/
body: Condition: derive the surface pronunciation of `/국민/` ('citizen', 6 phonemes) and `/국화/` ('chrysanthemum', 5 phonemes, counted on the basis of simple vowels excluding glides).

Step 1: In `/국민/`, the velar stop 'ㄱ' changes into the nasal 'ㅇ' before the nasal 'ㅁ', giving `[궁민]` (substitution). Step 2: In `/국화/`, 'ㄱ' and 'ㅎ' combine into the aspirated 'ㅋ', giving `[구콰]` (coalescence).
Interpretation: In `[궁민]` only substitution occurs, so the number of phonemes remains 6, but in `[구콰]` consonant coalescence occurs and the number of phonemes decreases by one.

examples.title: Multi-step derivation of /겉옷/ and /밭이랑/ (a furrow of a field)
body: Condition: derive the pronunciation of the compound words `/겉옷/` ('outer garment') and `/밭이랑/` (lexical morpheme '밭' + lexical morpheme '이랑').

Step 1: In `/겉옷/`, the syllable-final neutralization rule (substitution) applies to both roots, giving `/걷옫/`, and then liaison gives `[거돋]` (palatalization does not apply). Step 2: Since `/밭이랑/` is a combination of lexical morphemes, instead of palatalization, the syllable-final neutralization rule and n-insertion occur, giving `/받니랑/`, and then nasalization (substitution) gives `[반니랑]`.

Interpretation: Even when the second element begins with '이', if it is a lexical morpheme, palatalization does not occur, and the syllable-final neutralization rule, n-insertion, and nasalization apply in sequence.

kl-08.title: Morphological Analysis and Allomorph Alternation: Phonological and Morphological Conditions
explain: A **morpheme** (형태소) is the smallest unit of language that has meaning. According to whether it can be used alone, morphemes divide into **free morphemes** (자립형태소: nouns, pronouns, numerals, determiners, adverbs, interjections) and **bound morphemes** (의존형태소: particles, verb and adjective stems and endings, affixes); and according to whether they carry the lexical meaning of a concrete object or action, they are cross-classified into **lexical morphemes** (실질형태소: all free morphemes plus predicate stems) and **grammatical morphemes** (형식형태소: particles, endings, affixes).

Particular attention should be paid to the **stems of predicates** (용언의 어간; the '먹-' of '먹-다', the '예쁘-' of '예쁘-다'). A predicate stem carries substantive lexical meaning and so is a **lexical morpheme**, but since it cannot be used alone in a sentence without an ending, it is a **bound morpheme**. Conversely, a particle is a bound, grammatical morpheme that attaches only after a word that can stand alone, but in the Korean classification of parts of speech it is recognized as a **word**, on the grounds that it is easily separated from the freely standing word before it.

When a single morpheme is realized with different sounds depending on its surroundings, each of its forms is called an **allomorph** (이형태). Allomorph alternation is divided broadly into two conditions. First, there are **phonologically conditioned allomorphs**, which can be predicted regularly from the sounds before and after (whether it follows a consonant or a vowel, a yang vowel or a yin vowel). Representative are the nominative particle `이/가`, the accusative particle `을/를`, the auxiliary particle `은/는`, and the connective ending `-아/-어`.

Second, there are **morphologically (lexically) conditioned allomorphs**, which cannot be explained by phonological environment alone and are chosen exceptionally only after particular morphemes (words or stems). Examples are the case where, after the pronouns '나, 너, 저, 누구', the nominative particle meets '가' and the form of the pronoun changes; the case where only after the stem `'하-'` the form **`-여`** ('하여') is used instead of the ending `-아/-어`; and the case where after `'오-'` the imperative ending **`-너라`** ('오너라') is used.

Which of several allomorphs to take as the **basic form** (기본형, underlying form) is decided by economy of description and explanatory power. For example, the stem '먹-' is realized as [먹고, 먹어, 멍는다]; if `[먹]` is taken as the basic form, `[멍]` before a nasal can be explained by a single general phonological rule (nasalization), but if `[멍]` is taken as the basic form, it cannot be explained why it becomes 'ㄱ' before a vowel or 'ㄱ', so `/먹-/` becomes the basic form.

examples.title: Morpheme and word analysis of the sentence '하늘이 푸르다' ('The sky is blue')
body: Condition: divide the sentence `하늘이 푸르다` into morphemes and words, and determine the independence and the semantic nature of each morpheme.

Step 1: The morphemes are four in all: `하늘 / 이 / 푸르- / -다`. For words, since particles are recognized as words and stem plus ending ('푸르다') are bundled as one word, there are three in all: `하늘 / 이 / 푸르다`.
Step 2: They are classified as `하늘` (free, lexical), `이` (bound, grammatical), `푸르-` (bound, lexical), and `-다` (bound, grammatical).
Interpretation: One must correctly distinguish the category that is both a bound morpheme and a lexical morpheme, like the predicate stem `푸르-`.

examples.title: Determining the alternation condition of the allomorphs '-아 / -어 / -여'
body: Condition: compare the alternation conditions of the endings `-아/-어/-여` used in `잡-아`, `먹-어`, and `하-여`.
Step 1: `잡-아` (after the yang vowel ㅏ) and `먹-어` (after the yin vowel ㅓ) are determined by the nature of the stem-final vowel (vowel harmony), so they are phonologically conditioned allomorphs.

Step 2: By contrast, in `하-여`, even though the stem vowel is the yang vowel 'ㅏ', '-아' is not used and '-여' is chosen only after the particular stem `'하-'`, so it is a morphologically conditioned allomorph.
Interpretation: Even within the same class of morphemes, phonologically conditioned and morphologically conditioned allomorphs can exist together.

kl-09.title: Word Formation: Derived and Compound Words and Immediate Constituent (IC) Analysis
explain: Words divide into **simple words** (단일어) made of a single root ('하늘' 'sky', '바다' 'sea') and **complex words** (복합어) made by combining two or more morphemes. Complex words are in turn distinguished into **derived words** (파생어), in which a derivational affix (prefix or suffix) is attached to a root ('맨손' 'bare hand', '먹이' 'feed'), and **compound words** (합성어), in which two or more substantive roots are combined ('논밭' 'fields', '돌다리' 'stone bridge').

The prefixes that form **derived words** ('맨-', '풋-', '군-') are **restrictive affixes** (한정적 접사): they always attach before a root, only limit its meaning, and do not change the word's part of speech. Suffixes, by contrast, include restrictive suffixes that only add meaning ('선생-님'), but widely used are **governing affixes** (지배적 접사), which change the part of speech and syntactic structure of the root, as when `'-이'` attaches to the verb stem `'먹-'` to make the noun `'먹이'`, or `'-스럽-'` attaches to the noun `'사랑'` ('love') to make the adjective `'사랑스럽다'` ('lovable').

**Compound words** are divided, according to the semantic relation between the two roots, into coordinate compounds ('논밭', '오가다' 'come and go'), subordinate compounds ('돌다리', '국밥' 'rice soup'), and fused compounds ('춘추' [age], '밤낮' [always]); and, according to whether the manner of combination matches the general manner of sentence construction in Korean (word order, connective endings), into **syntactic compounds** (통사적 합성어) and **non-syntactic compounds** (비통사적 합성어). For example, `'작은형'` ('elder brother', containing the adnominal ending '-은'), `'돌아가다'` ('to turn back/pass away', containing the connective ending '-아'), and `'밤낮'` (noun + noun) are syntactic compounds.

By contrast, `'덮밥'` ('rice bowl dish'), `'접칼'` ('folding knife'), and `'검버섯'` ('age spots'), in which a verb stem is attached directly to a noun without an adnominal ending; `'오르내리다'` ('go up and down') and `'굶주리다'` ('starve'), in which two stems are attached directly without a connective ending; and `'척척박사'` ('know-it-all') and `'산들바람'` ('breeze'), in which an adverb directly modifies a noun, go against the general sentence word order and combination rules of Korean, and so are classified as **non-syntactic compounds**.

For complex words in which three or more morphemes are combined, whether the word is a derived word or a compound word is determined through **immediate constituent (IC) analysis** (직접구성성분 분석), which splits the word in two at the last stage at which the word was formed. For example, `'비웃음'` ('ridicule') splits as `[비웃- + -음]`, since the noun-deriving suffix `'-음'` is attached to the verb `'비웃-'` (비-+웃-), so it is a **derived word**. By contrast, `'눈물겹다'` ('moving, touching') splits as `[눈물 + -겹-]`, since the suffix `'-겹-'` is attached to the compound noun `'눈물'` (눈+물, 'tears'), so this too is a **derived word**, while `'나들이옷'` ('outing clothes') is `[나들이 + 옷]`, a combination of the derived noun `'나들이'` and the root `'옷'`, so it is a **compound word**.

examples.title: Comparing the IC analysis of '헛웃음' and '비웃음'
body: Condition: split `헛웃음` ('empty laugh') and `비웃음` ('ridicule'), each made of three morphemes, into immediate constituents (IC) and compare their structures.
Step 1: Because the verb `'헛웃다'` is not widely used, and the prefix `'헛-'` modifies the derived noun `'웃음'` (웃-+-음), `'헛웃음'` is analyzed as `[헛- + [웃- + -음]]` (a prefixal derived word).

Step 2: By contrast, in `'비웃음'` the verb `'비웃다'` (비-+웃-) exists first, and the nominalizing suffix `'-음'` is added to it to mean 'the act of ridiculing', so it is analyzed as `[[비- + 웃-] + -음]` (a suffixal derived word).
Interpretation: Even though they look identical in the order 'prefix + root + suffix', the IC structure differs according to the actual path of word formation and the semantic agreement.

examples.title: The syntactic compound '건널목' and the non-syntactic compound '꺾꽂이'
body: Condition: analyze the manner of combination of the roots in `건널목` ('crossing') and `꺾꽂이` ('cutting propagation').

Step 1: `건널목` has the adnominal ending `-ㄹ` attached to the verb stem `건너-` and then combines with the noun `목` (`건널 + 목`), so it is a syntactic compound that follows the normal Korean construction of modifier + noun.

Step 2: In `꺾꽂이`, the suffix `-이` is attached to `꺾꽂-`, in which the verb stems `꺾-` and `꽂-` are combined directly without the connective ending `-어` (`[[꺾- + 꽂-] + -이]`), so the internal stem combination is a non-syntactic compound, and the word as a whole is a suffixal derived word.
Interpretation: Only by distinguishing whether an ending intervenes and what the last stage of combination is (compounding vs. derivation) can the exact word structure be grasped.

kl-10.title: Korean Syntax: Predicate Valency and the Five Types of Embedded Sentences
explain: The number of obligatory sentence components that a predicate necessarily requires for a sentence to be grammatically complete is called the **valency of the predicate** (서술어의 자릿수, argument structure). Predicates divide into **one-place predicates**, which require only a subject ('꽃이 피다' 'A flower blooms'); **two-place predicates**, which require, besides the subject, one of an object, a complement, or an obligatory adverbial ('철수가 밥을 먹다' 'Cheolsu eats a meal', '물이 얼음이 되다' 'Water turns into ice', '영희가 어머니와 닮다' 'Yeonghui resembles her mother'); and **three-place predicates**, which require all three of subject, object, and obligatory adverbial ('삼촌이 나에게 책을 주다' 'My uncle gives me a book', '그가 영희를 제자로 삼다' 'He takes Yeonghui as his pupil').

A sentence in which the subject-predicate relation is established only once is called a **simple sentence** (홑문장), and one in which it is established two or more times is called a **complex sentence** (겹문장). Among complex sentences, a sentence in which one clause has entered another sentence as one of its components (subject, object, adnominal, adverbial, predicate) is called an **embedding sentence** (안은문장, embedded sentence), and the clause that has entered it is called an **embedded clause** (안긴절).

explain.alt: A table summarizing, for the five types of Korean embedding sentences (noun clause, adnominal clause, adverbial clause, predicate clause, quotative clause), the clause marker, the function within the sentence, and a representative example sentence
explain.caption: An embedded clause functions as a particular component of the sentence by means of a transformative ending or a quotative particle.

explain: There are five kinds of embedded clauses in Korean. (1) **Noun clause**: the nominalizing transformative ending `-(으)ㅁ, -기` attaches and the clause is used as a subject, object, or adverbial (`[봄이 옴]을 알았다` 'I knew that spring was coming'). (2) **Adnominal clause**: the adnominalizing transformative ending `-(으)ㄴ, -는, -(으)ㄹ, -던` attaches and the clause modifies the following noun (`[내가 읽은] 책` 'the book that I read'). (3) **Adverbial clause**: `-이, -게, -도록` and the like attach and the clause modifies a predicate (`비가 [소리도 없이] 내린다` 'The rain falls without a sound'). (4) **Predicate clause**: with no separate clause marker, the whole clause in the form `NP1은 [NP2가 VP]` serves as the predicate of the embedding sentence (`코끼리는 [코가 길다]` 'An elephant has a long trunk'). (5) **Quotative clause**: the quotative adverbial particle `고` (indirect quotation) or `라고` (direct quotation) attaches.

**Adnominal clauses** divide into two kinds according to whether a component inside the embedded clause has been omitted because it is identical to the head noun (the noun being modified). A case like `[내가 (책을) 읽은] 책`, where the object has been omitted, is called a **relative adnominal clause** (관계관형절, relative clause), and a case like `[그가 범인이라는] 사실` ('the fact that he is the culprit'), where no component has been omitted and the content of the whole clause and the head noun ('사실' 'fact', '소문' 'rumor', '기억' 'memory') refer to the same content, is called an **appositive adnominal clause** (동격관형절, complement-noun clause).

There are also limits and points of caution. Even in a sentence that appears to have the particle `'이/가'` twice, if the predicate is `'되다'` or `'아니다'`, the first noun phrase is the subject and the latter is a **complement** (보어), so it is not a complex sentence embedding a predicate clause but a **simple sentence with a two-place predicate** (`물이 얼음이 되었다`). Therefore one should not merely count the number of '이/가', but consider how many times a subject-predicate relation holds.

examples.title: Determining the syntax of '물이 얼음이 되었다' and '토끼는 앞발이 짧다'
body: Condition: determine, through predicate valency, whether the two sentences are simple sentences or complex sentences embedding a predicate clause.

Step 1: In `물이 얼음이 되었다` ('The water turned into ice'), the predicate `되다` is a two-place predicate requiring a subject (`물이`) and a complement (`얼음이`), so the subject-predicate relation holds only once and it is a **simple sentence**.

Step 2: In `토끼는 앞발이 짧다` ('A rabbit has short forelegs'), the adjective `짧다` is a one-place predicate taking `앞발이` as its subject, and the whole clause `[앞발이 짧다]` serves as the predicate of the overall subject `토끼는`, so it is a **complex sentence embedding a predicate clause**.
Interpretation: Whether there is a predicate clause must be verified by predicate valency and the number of subject-predicate agreements.

examples.title: Distinguishing relative and appositive adnominal clauses
body: Condition: compare the internal structure of the adnominal clauses in `[형님이 주신] 시계` ('the watch that my elder brother gave') and `[친구가 합격했다는] 소식` ('the news that my friend passed').
Step 1: In `[형님이 (시계를) 주신] 시계`, the object of the embedded clause (`시계를`) is the same as the head noun being modified (`시계`) and has been omitted, so it is a **relative adnominal clause**.
Step 2: In `[친구가 합격했다는] 소식`, the sentence `친구가 합격했다` lacks no obligatory component, and the content of that clause coincides with the content of `소식`, so it is an **appositive adnominal clause**.
Interpretation: If the head noun can be put back into the embedded clause as a subject, object, or adverbial, it is a relative adnominal clause; if it cannot, it is an appositive adnominal clause.

kl-11.title: Korean Semantics and Pragmatics: The Honorific System, Tense and Aspect, Indirect Speech Acts
explain: Korean **honorifics** (높임법) operate along three axes according to whom the speaker elevates. First, **subject honorifics** (주체 높임법), which elevate the subject of the sentence, are realized mainly by the pre-final ending **`-(으)시-`**, the nominative particle `께서`, and special vocabulary (`계시다` 'be (honorific)', `잡수시다` 'eat (honorific)', `주무시다` 'sleep (honorific)'). Second, **object honorifics** (객체 높임법), which elevate the referent of an object or adverbial, are realized by the particle **`께`** and special vocabulary (`모시다` 'accompany', `뵙다` 'meet', `드리다` 'give', `여쭙다` 'ask'). Third, **addressee honorifics** (상대 높임법), which elevate the listener (addressee), are realized by sentence-final endings in six levels: formal styles (hasipsio-che 하십시오체, hao-che 하오체, hage-che 하게체, haera-che 해라체) and informal styles (haeyo-che 해요체, hae-che 해체).

Subject honorification includes **direct honorification** (직접 높임), which elevates the person who is the subject directly (`선생님께서 웃으신다` 'The teacher smiles'), and **indirect honorification** (간접 높임), which elevates indirectly through a part of the body, a possession, a thought, and so on of the person who should be elevated (`교장 선생님 말씀이 있으시겠습니다` 'The principal will give some remarks', `할머니께서는 귀가 밝으시다` 'Grandmother has sharp ears'). The key grammatical constraint is that in indirect honorification the special vocabulary `'계시다'` is not used, and **`'있으시다'`** is used instead.

Temporal expression divides into **tense** (시제), which indicates the before-and-after relation between the time of utterance (the moment of speaking) and the time of the event (the moment the event occurred) (past `-았-/-었-`, present `-는-/-ㄴ-`, future `-겠-/-리-`), and **aspect** (동작상), which indicates whether an action is in progress or completed in the flow of time (progressive `-고 있다`, perfective `-아/-어 있다`). The pre-final ending `-았-/-었-` expresses not only past tense but also completion or certainty (`내일 소풍은 다 갔다` 'Tomorrow's picnic is as good as gone'), and `-겠-` expresses, besides future tense, **modality** (양태) meanings such as conjecture (`지금쯤 도착했겠다` 'It must have arrived by now') or the subject's volition (`제가 하겠습니다` 'I will do it').

**Pragmatics** (화용론) investigates how the literal meaning of a sentence (propositional meaning) is interpreted within the context of utterance as the speaker's intention (illocutionary force). When sentence type (declarative, interrogative, imperative, propositive) and the purpose of the utterance (statement, question, request, promise) match, it is a **direct speech act**, and when they do not match, it is an **indirect speech act**. For example, in a cold room with an open window, saying `"방이 좀 춥네"` ('It's a bit cold in here', a declarative) or `"창문 좀 닫아 줄래?"` ('Would you close the window?', an interrogative) to convey a **request (command)** to close the window is an indirect speech act.

Paul Grice explained that, on the assumption that participants in conversation observe the **cooperative principle** (the maxims of quantity, quality, relation, and manner), a hearer infers the hidden intention, the **conversational implicature**, from an utterance that seems on the surface to violate a maxim. Also, in politeness theory, indirect speech acts are widely used instead of direct commands in order to give the other party a choice without threatening that party's face.

examples.title: Analysis of triple honorification in a single sentence
body: Condition: find all the subject, object, and addressee honorific elements appearing in the sentence `"어머니, 할머니께 선물을 드리셨어요?"` ('Mother, did you give Grandmother a present?').
Step 1: To elevate the subject (Mother), the pre-final ending **`-시-`** is used (`드리-시-었-어요`) (subject honorific).

Step 2: To elevate the adverbial referent (Grandmother), the particle **`께`** and the special verb **`드리다`** are used (object honorific), and to elevate the addressee (Mother), the informal honorific sentence-final ending **`-어요`** (haeyo-che) is used (addressee honorific).
Interpretation: In a single predicate, the object honorific vocabulary (`드리-`), the subject honorific pre-final ending (`-시-`), and the addressee honorific ending (`-어요`) combine in sequence.

examples.title: Judging the well-formedness of indirect honorification: '계시다' vs '있으시다'
body: Condition: analyze the difference between `"선생님께서 교무실에 계신다"` ('The teacher is in the staff room') and `"선생님께서 시간이 있으시다 / *계시다"` ('The teacher has time').
Step 1: The subject of the first sentence is `선생님` ('teacher') himself, so the direct-honorific special vocabulary `계시다` is used.

Step 2: In the second sentence, the direct subject of the predicate `있다` is not the teacher but `시간` ('time'), something owned by or related to the teacher, so it is an indirect-honorific environment. Therefore `계시다` is ungrammatical and `있으시다` must be used.

Interpretation: Saying `"주문하신 커피 나오셨습니다"` ('Your ordered coffee has come out (honorific)'), elevating goods or coffee, is excessive honorification (misuse), using `-시-` on a thing that is not an object of elevation.

kl-12.title: The Creation Principles of Hunminjeongeum and Features of Middle Korean Phonology and Grammar
explain: **Hunminjeongeum** (훈민정음, 訓民正音), created by King Sejong in 1443 and promulgated in 1446, is an original phonemic script modeled on the speech organs and the principles of the cosmos. For the **17 initial consonant letters**, five basic letters (**ㄱ, ㄴ, ㅁ, ㅅ, ㅇ**) were first made by the **principle of pictography** (상형, 象形), imitating the shapes of the speech organs; the remaining letters (ㅋ, ㄷ·ㅌ, ㅂ·ㅍ, ㅈ·ㅊ, ㆆ·ㅎ) were made from these by the **principle of stroke addition** (가획, 加劃), adding strokes according to the strength of the sound (plain sound → aspirated sound, and so on); and letters that departed from stroke addition were set apart as **variant letters** (이체자: ㄹ, ㅿ, ㆁ).

For the **11 medial vowel letters**, the three basic letters (**·, ㅡ, ㅣ**), modeled on the three powers of heaven (·, a round shape), earth (ㅡ, a flat shape), and humans (ㅣ, a standing shape), were made by pictography, and by the **principle of combination** (합용, 合用), which joins these with one another, the first-derived letters (초출자: ㅗ, ㅏ, ㅜ, ㅓ) and the second-derived letters (재출자: ㅛ, ㅑ, ㅠ, ㅕ) were made. For **final consonants**, no new letters were made, and the principle of **final consonants reusing initial consonants** (종성부용초성, 終聲復用初聲) was established, whereby the initial consonant letters are written again.

The phonological system of 15th-century **Middle Korean** was clearly different from that of Modern Korean. There existed phonemes that have since disappeared: the labial-fricative bieup (`ㅸ`), the semi-dental (`ㅿ`), the old ieung (`ㆁ`), the light hieut (`ㆆ`), and the vowel **arae-a (`ㆍ`)**; **word-initial consonant clusters** (어두자음군: `ㅳ, ㅼ, ㅶ`, etc.) were actually pronounced; and it was a **tone language** (성조, 聲調), distinguishing pitch with dots (방점) placed to the left of the letter (one dot for the high tone, two dots for the rising tone, none for the low tone). In addition, **vowel harmony** (모음조화), in which yang vowels (`ㆍ, ㅗ, ㅏ`) go with yang vowels and yin vowels (`ㅡ, ㅜ, ㅓ`) with yin vowels, was observed far more strictly than in the modern language.

In orthography, **continuous writing** (이어적기, 連綴: writing as it sounds, with the final consonant carried over to the next syllable; e.g. `깊+어 → 기퍼` 'deep', `말ᄊᆞᆷ+이 → 말ᄊᆞ미` 'word(s)') was universal, and the **eight-final-consonant rule** (8종성가족용), which uses only the eight letters 'ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㆁ' for finals, was applied, so that the pronunciations of 'ㅅ' and 'ㄷ' finals were distinguished.

Grammar also shows features different from Modern Korean. First, the nominative particle `'가'` was not yet used, and only `'이'` after a consonant (`말ᄊᆞ미`), `'ㅣ'` after a vowel (`부텨+ㅣ → 부톄`), or a zero form (`∅`, after the vowel 'ㅣ') appeared. Second, the object honorific was realized regularly by the pre-final ending **`-삽-/-잡-/-습-`**. Third, in interrogative sentences, the endings were precisely differentiated: when the subject was second person, `-니가/-니아` was used, and when it was first or third person, yes-no questions (`-가/-아`) and wh-questions (`-고/-오`) were distinguished.

examples.title: Classifying the creation principles of Hunminjeongeum initials and medials
body: Condition: classify the principles by which the consonants `ㄴ, ㄷ, ㅌ, ㄹ` and the vowels `ㆍ, ㅡ, ㅗ, ㅛ` were made.

Step 1: `ㄴ` is a **basic letter** (pictographic) modeled on the shape of the tongue tip touching the upper gum ridge; `ㄷ` and `ㅌ` are **stroke-added letters** made by adding one stroke each to `ㄴ`; and `ㄹ` is a **variant letter** to which the meaning of stroke addition (strength of sound) does not apply.

Step 2: `ㆍ` and `ㅡ` are **basic letters** (pictographic) modeled on heaven and earth; `ㅗ` is a **first-derived letter** (combination) made by joining `ㆍ` and `ㅡ` once; and `ㅛ` is a **second-derived letter** (combination) made by joining `ㆍ` to `ㅗ` once more.
Interpretation: The core design of Hunminjeongeum is to make a minimal set of basic letters by pictography and expand the system by stroke addition (consonants) and combination (vowels).

examples.title: Analysis of the 15th-century Middle Korean phrase '말ᄊᆞ미 듕귁에 달아'
body: Condition: compare `'말ᄊᆞ미 듕귁에 달아'` from the Hunminjeongeum Eonhaebon (the vernacular translation) with Modern Korean `'말씀이 중국과 달라'` ('the language is different from China's').
Step 1: `'말ᄊᆞ미'` is the noun `'말ᄊᆞᆷ'` combined with the nominative particle `'이'`, written as it sounds by **continuous writing** (이어적기).

Step 2: In `'듕귁에'`, palatalization had not yet occurred, so it is written `'듕'`; **`'에'`** is used as the comparative adverbial particle instead of the modern `'과/와'`; and `'달아'` (`다ᄅᆞ- + -아`) still shows the `'ㄹㅇ'` conjugation rather than the `'ㄹㄹ'` conjugation.

Interpretation: Even within one short phrase, one can read continuous writing, the state before palatalization, the difference in meaning of the adverbial particle, and the diachronic change in predicate conjugation.

kl-13.title: Metrical and Formal Change in Classical Korean Poetry: Hyangga, Goryeo Songs, Sijo, and Gasa
explain: The history of classical Korean poetry has developed its own distinctive **meter** (율격; foot-based and syllable-count-based rhythm) and **line and verse structure** in step with changes in the means of notation (borrowed Chinese characters → Hangul) and in the classes that enjoyed it (monks and hwarang → the Goryeo court and the common people → Joseon literati, gisaeng, and commoners). **Hyangga** (향가, 鄕歌), which reached its peak in the Silla period after the ancient songs, was recorded in **hyangchal** (향찰, 鄕札), a script that borrowed the sounds and meanings of Chinese characters to write in Korean word order, and passed through the 4-line and 8-line forms to settle in its most complete form, the **10-line hyangga** (e.g. Jemangmaega 제망매가, Chan Giparangga 찬기파랑가).

The 10-line hyangga takes, in content and form, a **three-part structure** of `4 lines + 4 lines + 2 lines`, and has the rule of placing an **exclamation** such as `'아으'` or `'아야'` at the head of the last two lines, the **nakgu** (落句, lines 9 and 10), to concentrate and turn the poetic thought. This three-part structure and the tradition of an exclamation at the head of the nakgu are judged to have been the origin of the later representative fixed-form poem of late Goryeo and Joseon, the **sijo** (시조: a three-verse structure of first, second, and final verse, with the first foot of the final verse fixed at three syllables).

explain.alt: A table comparing the four classical Korean poetic genres (10-line hyangga, Goryeo songs, pyeongsijo, gasa) by script of notation, basic meter, and the rules for the final verse or nakgu
explain.caption: The nakgu rule of the 10-line hyangga continues in the final verse of sijo and the closing lines of regular gasa.

explain: The **Goryeo songs** (고려가요, also called Goryeo sokyo: Gasiri 가시리, Cheongsanbyeolgok 청산별곡, Seogyeongbyeolgok 서경별곡, etc.) of the Goryeo period are a genre in which the orally transmitted folk songs of commoners were taken up as court banquet music and then fixed in writing after the creation of Hangul in the Joseon period. Goryeo songs have as their basis a **`3-foot`** (`3·3·2` pattern, etc.) meter, and developed a **stanzaic form** (분연체) in which several stanzas follow one another, and varied **refrains and vocables** fitted to the musical rhythm (`얄리얄리 얄랑셩`, `위 두어렁셩 두어렁셩 다링디리`).

The **sijo** (시조, 時調), which started with the new literati class in late Goryeo and spread to all classes in the Joseon period, has a **`4-foot`** meter and a strict fixed form of **three verses (first, second, and final) and six lines, of about 45 syllables**. In particular, the key rule is that **the first foot of the final verse is always fixed at three syllables** and the second foot is stretched long to five syllables or more (`3·5·4·3`). In late Joseon the **sasol sijo** (사설시조), in which the second verse becomes much longer and lists everyday language, appeared, and **gasa** (歌辭), a continuous series of 4-foot lines chanted at length without limit on the number of lines, developed into **regular gasa** (정격가사: Gwandongbyeolgok 관동별곡, Samiingok 사미인곡) if its last line kept the sijo final-verse form (`3·5·4·3`), and into **irregular gasa** (변격가사) if it did not keep it and contained the realities of commoners and women.

examples.title: Reading the 3-foot meter of Goryeo songs and the 4-foot meter of sijo by foot breaks
body: Condition: analyze the feet of the Goryeo song `'가시리 가시리잇고 나ᄂᆞᆫ'` ('Are you leaving, are you leaving? As for me') and the pyeongsijo `'동짓달 기나긴 밤을 한 허리를 베어 내어'` ('Cutting out a waist of the long winter-solstice night').
Step 1: Excluding the vocable (`나ᄂᆞᆫ`), the Goryeo song is read in breaks as `'가시리 / 가시리 / 잇고'` (`3·3·2`), a **3-foot** meter.
Step 2: The pyeongsijo is a **4-foot** meter, in which one verse (line) breaks into four chunks, as in `'동짓달 / 기나긴 밤을 / 한 허리를 / 베어 내어'` (`3·5·4·4`).
Interpretation: The lively 3-foot meter of the Goryeo songs shifted, in the poetry of the Joseon literati (sijo and gasa), to the stable 4-foot meter.

examples.title: Contrasting the final verse of sijo and the last line of regular gasa
body: Condition: look at the closing lines of regular gasa such as the one before the last line `'님다히 소식을 아무려나 아자 하니'` of Jeong Cheol's gasa 〈Samiingok〉 and the closing of 〈Gwandongbyeolgok〉, such as `'밝은 달이 천산만락에 아니 비친 데 없다'`.
Step 1: The closing of 〈Samiingok〉, `'각시님 / 달이야카니와 / 궂은비나 / 되쇼셔'`, has a syllable count of `3 / 6 / 4 / 3`, with the first foot at three syllables and the second foot at five syllables or more.

Step 2: This corresponds exactly to the essential rule of the pyeongsijo final verse, **`first foot fixed at 3 syllables + second foot of 5 syllables or more`**, so it is judged to be **regular gasa**.
Interpretation: Gasa is a continuous series of 4-foot lines of unlimited length, but by sharing the form of the sijo final verse in its closing (last line), it shows its generic kinship with sijo.

kl-14.title: Oral Literature and the Narrative Aesthetics of Pansori: Chang and Aniri, Imyeon and Elaboration
explain: **Oral literature** (구비문학, 口碑文學: folktales, folk songs, shaman songs, pansori, folk drama) is an art of the spoken word transmitted from mouth to mouth rather than recorded in writing. Unlike written literature, in which a single author leaves a fixed text, oral literature is **cumulative literature** (적층문학, 積層文學) and has the character of **collective authorship**, recreated anew each time through the interaction of the performer (speaker) and the audience at the site of performance.

**Pansori** (판소리), the crystallization of commoner art in late Joseon, is a dramatic narrative epic in which a single **sorikkun** (소리꾼: singer, or gwangdae) recounts a long story to the rhythm of a **gosu** (고수: the drummer), mixing **chang** (창: sung passages), **aniri** (아니리: spoken passages), and **ballim** (발림, also neoleumsae: gestures). The gosu and the audience are not mere spectators but take part directly in the narrative, adding **chuimsae** (추임새: encouraging interjections) such as `'얼씨구'` and `'좋다'` to lift the spirit of the performance.

The rhythmic patterns (장단) of pansori are finely alternated from slow to fast according to the emotions of the characters and the tension of the events. The slowest, most plaintive or sorrowful passages use **jinyangjo** (진양조), calm narration uses **jungmori** (중모리), lively or comic passages use **jungjungmori** (중중모리), and the most urgent, rushing scenes (for example, the Royal Inspector's arrival, or the scene of Nolbu splitting open the gourds) use the **jajinmori and hwimori (자진모리·휘모리)** rhythms. The aesthetic principle of realizing sound and rhythm to suit the meaning of the lyrics and the dramatic situation is called **drawing the imyeon** (이면, 裏面: the inner side).

Another key feature of pansori style is the **expansive style** (확장적 문체: elaboration, 치장, and deoneum, 더늠), in which, when a particular scene or object appears, the story line is briefly suspended and every available vocabulary and piece of knowledge is poured out rhythmically. Through contrasting Sino-Korean idioms and listings of classical allusions (고사), **enumeration and parallelism** that list similar things endlessly, and a combination of wordplay and the comic (humor and satire), the Chinese-style language of the yangban and the vulgar language of the commoners collide and mix within one work.

This dual-language structure is directly tied to the **duality of theme** of pansori (the surface theme and the underlying theme). For example, 〈Chunhyangga〉 (춘향가) puts forward on the surface the Confucian **'chastity of a virtuous woman (烈女)'** (surface theme, the demand of the yangban class), but inwardly it holds **'liberation from status and criticism of corrupt officials'** (underlying theme, the desire of the commoner class), as Chunhyang, the daughter of a gisaeng, tries to cross the barrier of the status system and attain human liberation and love. It is a composite aesthetic born of the reality of the gwangdae, who had to draw both yangban and commoners in as audience.

examples.title: Analysis of how pansori rhythms combine with the dramatic situation (imyeon)
body: Condition: match rhythms to two passages of 〈Chunhyangga〉: (1) the passage in which Chunhyang, imprisoned, laments in longing for her beloved (the prison song, 옥중가), and (2) the passage in which Yi Mongnyong appears as the secret royal inspector and the post-runners burst into the magistrate's hall (the Royal Inspector's arrival, 어사출두).
Step 1: Since passage (1) centers on a tragic and sorrowful mood, the sound is drawn out long in the slowest and most plaintive **jinyangjo** rhythm.
Step 2: Since passage (2) is an urgent situation in which events rush like a storm, tension is maximized with the fastest **jajinmori and hwimori** rhythms and breathless enumerative phrases.
Interpretation: In pansori, the choice of rhythm is not mere beat-keeping but a core device for giving form to narrative tension and the characters' inner side (imyeon).

examples.title: The dual structure of surface theme and underlying theme (Heungbuga)
body: Condition: compare the theme of the pansori 〈Heungbuga〉 (흥보가) at the level of yangban morality and at the level of late Joseon economic reality.

Step 1: On the surface, it puts forward the Confucian and moral **brotherly affection and the encouragement of good and punishment of evil** (surface theme), in which brothers are fond of each other and good people are rewarded.

Step 2: Beneath the surface, through the opposition between Heungbo, a fallen yangban and poor farmer, and Nolbu, who monopolizes wealth through rich farming and commercial capital, it satirizes the **shaking of the status system, the gap between rich and poor, and the contradictions of the money economy** in late Joseon (underlying theme).
Interpretation: Because Confucian instruction and the commoners' criticism of reality coexist in a single work, pansori could win broad support from all classes.

kl-15.title: The Development of the Classical Korean Novel: Chuanqi, Heroic, and Family Novels and Pansori-Based Novels
explain: The classical Korean novel was established as a full-fledged fictional genre, passing through the stepping stone of the **gajeon** (假傳: personified-object biographies, such as Guksunjeon and Gongbangjeon) of late Goryeo, in Kim Si-seup's 15th-century **Geumo Sinhwa** (《금오신화》, New Tales of Mt. Geumo; Manboksa jopogi, Iseng gyujangjeon, etc.). The **chuanqi novel** (전기소설, 傳奇小說) represented by Geumo Sinhwa is a Chinese-character novel in which a gifted scholar (才子) and a beautiful woman (佳人) move back and forth between unreal, transcendent worlds (death, the Dragon Palace, the underworld) and share a tragic love, giving form to the inner life of a solitary individual confronting the tyranny of the world.

After the 17th century, going through the historical shock of the Imjin War and the Byeongja War, Hangul novels and **heroic novels** (영웅소설: Honggildongjeon, Yuchungnyeoljeon, Jo Ungjeon, etc.) became explosively popular. Heroic novels share the typical **structure of a hero's life story** (영웅의 일대기: (1) noble bloodline → (2) abnormal birth → (3) outstanding ability → (4) childhood trials, abandonment, and rescue → (5) help and upbringing by a helper → (6) after growing up, overcoming crises and victory through martial prowess), and carried the people's longing to be compensated, through the hero's exploits, for the sense of defeat in war and for social contradictions.

Meanwhile, centered on the yangban families and the readership of women in the inner quarters, **dream-journey and dream-framed novels** (몽유록·몽자류 소설: Guunmong, with its 'reality → dream → awakening' dream structure) and long **family novels** (가문소설: Sassi Namjeonggi, Changseon Gamuirok) dealing with a family's prosperity and conflict over several generations developed. In addition, in the 18th century Park Ji-won, a writer of the Silhak (practical learning) school, sharply satirized the hypocrisy and incompetence of the yangban class and the fictitiousness of the northern-expedition argument through short Chinese-character tales such as **〈Hojil〉, 〈Yangbanjeon〉, and 〈Heosaengjeon〉**, and presented the reformist idea of 'utilizing tools and enriching life' (利用厚生).

Amid the development of commerce in late Joseon and the spread of sechaekga (book-rental shops) and bangakbon (commercially printed editions), **pansori-based novels** (판소리계 소설: Chunhyangjeon, Simcheongjeon, Heungbujeon, Tokkijeon), in which orally transmitted pansori lyrics settled as reading material, rose to become the mainstream of commoner fiction. Unlike heroic novels, pansori-based novels reduced transcendent magic and the intervention of the heavenly realm, and depicted the worldly conflicts experienced by ordinary or deprived lower-class characters through **humor and satire** and a lively verse-like colloquial style, opening the way toward the modern realist novel.

The classical novel generally has the common features of a happy ending, an overabundance of coincidence, flat and typical characters, and a life-story temporal structure, but there are also abundant exceptional and innovative achievements, such as works like 〈Iseng gyujangjeon〉 and 〈Unyeongjeon〉 that take a **tragic ending** to denounce the oppression of fate and institutions, and pansori-based novels and Park Ji-won's short Chinese-character tales that realistically exposed the contradictions of their day.

examples.title: Comparing the narrative structure of 〈Honggildongjeon〉 and 〈Guunmong〉
body: Condition: compare the central narrative frames of Heo Gyun's 〈Honggildongjeon〉 and Kim Man-jung's 〈Guunmong〉.

Step 1: 〈Honggildongjeon〉 follows the **structure of a hero's life story**: born as the illegitimate son of a distinguished family (noble bloodline and deprivation), overcoming the threat of assassins (trials), leading the Hwalbindang with magic, and finally becoming king of Yuldo.

Step 2: 〈Guunmong〉 follows a **'reality → dream → reality' illusory-dream structure**: coming down from heaven (Seongjin) to the human world (Yang Soyu), enjoying wealth and glory, and then waking from the dream and returning to heaven (Seongjin).

Interpretation: If the hero's life story aims at the fulfillment of worldly desire and the resolution of social contradictions, the illusory-dream structure shows at the same time the emptiness that follows the fulfillment of worldly desire and a transcendent awakening.

examples.title: Contrasting the worldviews of heroic novels and pansori-based novels
body: Condition: compare how conflict is resolved in the military-tale heroic novel 〈Yuchungnyeoljeon〉 and the pansori-based novel 〈Heungbujeon〉.

Step 1: In 〈Yuchungnyeoljeon〉, in accordance with a fate decreed in the heavenly realm, the hero obtains a Taoist master and miraculous weapons, defeats the rebel army, and restores his family and the royal authority (a transcendent, dualistic worldview).

Step 2: In 〈Heungbujeon〉, Heungbu, a yangban but poor, lives amid the bottom-level economic reality of late Joseon, with day labor and selling himself to take beatings in another's place, and through commoner humor and the comic satirizes the greed of the rich farmer Nolbu (a realistic, empirical worldview).

Interpretation: As one moves toward late Joseon, the social and economic reality of the time and the voice of the commoners moved to the center of the novel, rather than the predestination of the heavenly realm.

kl-16.title: A History of Modern Korean Poetry: From Modern Lyric Poetry through Modernism and the Life School to Postwar and Minjung Poetry
explain: Modern Korean poetry passed through the **enlightenment-era gasa and changga** (개화가사·창가: external meter in 4·4 or 7·5 patterns) and Choe Nam-seon's **sinchesi** (신체시, 'new-style poetry'; 〈Haeege-seo sonyeonege〉), and from the end of the 1910s, with Ju Yo-han's 〈Bulnori〉 and Kim Eok's translated anthology 《Oenoe-ui mudo》 as starting points, was established as **free verse** (자유시, internal rhythm), freed from fixed external meter. In the early 1920s, sentimental romantic poetry was popular, centered on coterie magazines such as 《Baekjo》 and 《Pyeheo》, but soon the unrivaled achievements of three poets, who combined the traditional national meter with deep lyricism, appeared.

The three pillars of the 1920s are **Kim So-wol**, **Han Yong-un**, and (early) **Jeong Ji-yong**. In 《Jindallaekkot》 (Azaleas), Kim So-wol sublimated the sorrow (han, 恨) of parting into modern lyric poetry through the traditional **7·5 pattern, 3-foot folk-song meter** and a feminine tone; in 《Nim-ui chimmuk》 (The Silence of the Beloved), Han Yong-un turned the absence of the 'beloved' (the homeland, truth, sentient beings) into the hope of reunion through Buddhist **paradox** and a prose rhythm in the honorific style; and Jeong Ji-yong, who was active through the 1930s along with Baek Seok and Yi Yong-ak, restrained excess of emotion and opened the path of **sensory imagism**, capturing objects in vivid visual imagery.

The 1930s greatly broadened the horizon of modern poetry through the competition of the Poetry and Literature school (시문학파: Park Yong-cheol and Kim Yeong-rang, pure lyricism and the musical refinement of poetic diction); **modernism and intellectualism** (모더니즘·주지주의: Kim Gi-rim, Kim Gwang-gyun, and Yi Sang, with a pictorial sense of urban civilization and the dismantling of established modes of speech and the self); the **Life school** (생명파: Seo Jeong-ju and Yu Chi-hwan, who, reacting against the technicism of modernism, explored primal vitality and existential will); and the **vernacular-community and exile narrative poetry** of Baek Seok and Yi Yong-ak. In the dark period at the end of Japanese rule, the **Cheongnok school** (청록파: Jo Ji-hun, Park Mok-wol, and Park Du-jin, nature and traditional aesthetics), **Yun Dong-ju** (reflection on shame, and resistance), and **Yi Yuk-sa** (a strong masculine tone and the will to overcome) kept the spirit of poetry alive.

In the 1950s after liberation and the Korean War, modernism that sang of postwar ruin and existential anxiety (the Late-Period coterie) confronted the restoration of traditional lyricism; with the April 19 Revolution of the 1960s as the occasion, **Kim Su-yeong** (engaged poetry: exposing the vulgarity of daily life and a passionate prose rhythm toward freedom) and **Sin Dong-yeop** (national epic and earthly vitality) appeared and led the debate between pure and engaged poetry.

In the industrialization and democratization of the 1970s and 80s, the **minjung poetry and realist poetry** (민중시·현실주의 시) of Sin Gyeong-rim (〈Nongmu〉), Kim Ji-ha, Park No-hae, and others bore witness to the lives of marginalized farmers and workers, while Hwang Dong-gyu, Jeong Hyeon-jong, O Gyu-won, Gi Hyeong-do, and others broke through the oppressive era with **irony, allegory, and reflexive experiments on language itself**, deepening at once the aesthetic autonomy and the social engagement of modern poetry.

examples.title: Comparing the 3-foot folk meter of Kim So-wol's 〈Jindallaekkot〉 and the paradox of Han Yong-un's 〈Nim-ui chimmuk〉
body: Condition: compare the meter and rhetoric of the representative 1920s anthologies, Kim So-wol's 《Jindallaekkot》 and Han Yong-un's 《Nim-ui chimmuk》.

Step 1: 〈Jindallaekkot〉 (`나 보기가 / 역겨워 / 가실 때에는`, 'When you leave, sick of the sight of me', 7·5 pattern, 3 feet) holds the sorrow of parting inward through the 3-foot meter of traditional folk song and ironic expression (`죽어도 아니 눈물 흘리우리다`, 'Even if I die, I will not shed a tear').

Step 2: 〈Nim-ui chimmuk〉 (`아아, 님은 갔지마는 나는 님을 보내지 아니하였습니다`, 'Ah, though my beloved has gone, I have not sent my beloved away') turns absence into the will to overcome through a long-breathed prose-like internal rhythm and **paradox**, which holds truth within surface contradiction.

Interpretation: Though both belong to the same 1920s poetics of 'parting and absence', they form a clear contrast in meter (a leaning toward 3-foot fixed form vs. free prose rhythm) and in rhetoric (irony vs. paradox).

examples.title: Contrasting the poetics of the 1930s Poetry and Literature school, modernism, and Life school
body: Condition: compare the values most prized in poetry by Kim Yeong-rang (Poetry and Literature school), Kim Gi-rim and Yi Sang (modernism), and Seo Jeong-ju and Yu Chi-hwan (Life school).
Step 1: The Poetry and Literature school excluded political ideology and concentrated on refining the beautiful, delicate musical resonance of the Korean language and pure lyricism.

Step 2: Modernism rejected sentimental tears and captured modern urban civilization through visual imagery, intellect (intellectualism), and geometric dismantling, while the Life school, again opposing urban technicism, expressed intensely humanity's primal instincts and the anguish of life.
Interpretation: Korean modern poetry of the 1930s matured within a triangular structure of 'musical lyricism — visual and intellectual critique of civilization — exploration of primal life'.

kl-17.title: A History of the Modern Korean Novel: The Divergence of Realism and Modernism, and Narratives of Division and Industrialization
explain: The modern Korean novel passed through the **sinsoseol** (신소설, 'new novel': a transitional period toward unifying spoken and written language, with enlightenment and a coincidence-driven plot) of the enlightenment era, such as Yi In-jik's 〈Hyeorui nu〉, and announced its full-fledged start in 1917 with Yi Gwang-su's long novel **《Mujeong》** (The Heartless), which achieved the discovery of the modern individual and a refined prose style unifying spoken and written language. But it was from Kim Dong-in's activity in the coterie of 《Changjo》 in 1919 and the emergence of **realist fiction** in the 1920s that the enlightenment and preachy limits remaining in 《Mujeong》 were overcome and the autonomy of literature and realistic description were established.

Fiction of the 1920s developed in two broad currents. One was the individualist and realist literature represented by **Kim Dong-in** (〈Baettaragi〉, 〈Gamja〉), **Hyeon Jin-geon** (〈Unsu joeun nal〉, 〈Bincheo〉), and **Yeom Sang-seop** (〈Pyobonsil-ui cheonggaeguri〉, 〈Manseijeon〉), which captured human fate and poverty in colonial reality with a cool, objective gaze and irony. The other was the class-oriented literature of the **New Tendency school and KAPF** (the Korea Artista Proletaria Federatio), such as Choe Seo-hae (〈Talchulgi〉) and Jo Myeong-hui (〈Nakdonggang〉), which sought the causes of colonial exploitation and destitution in the contradictions of social structure and stirred a consciousness of resistance.

The 1930s were the period in which the modern Korean novel flowered most variously in method. **Yeom Sang-seop**'s 《Samdae》 (Three Generations) painted, panorama-like, colonial capitalism and the collapse of the family system through the conflict of three generations: grandfather, father, and grandson; **Chae Man-sik**'s 《Taepyeongcheonha》 and 〈Redimeideu insaeng〉 grafted pansori-like **satire and irony** onto the modern novel and scathingly criticized the downfall of the pro-Japanese landlord class and the unemployment of colonial intellectuals. At the same time, **Park Tae-won** (〈Soseolga Gubossi-ui ilil〉, with modernology (고현학) and the gaze of the flaneur) and **Yi Sang** (〈Nalgae〉, with the **stream-of-consciousness** technique and the fragmented modern self) showed the peak of the urban modernist novel, while Kim Yu-jeong, Yi Hyo-seok, Kim Jeong-han, and others gave original form to the vitality and pathos of rural and vernacular life.

Through the liberation period (Chae Man-sik's 〈Miseuteo Bang〉, Yi Tae-jun's 〈Haebang jeonhu〉) and the Korean War, the **postwar fiction** of the 1950s faced head-on the scars left by war and the destruction of humanity. Son Chang-seop and Jang Yong-hak depicted absurd existence, Yi Beom-seon (〈Obalt'an〉) and Ha Geun-chan (〈Sunan-idae〉) depicted the tragedy of war victims, and **Choe In-hun**'s **《Gwangjang》** (The Square, 1960), by criticizing both the licentious 'secret room' of South Korea and the uniform 'square' of North Korea and seeking a third, human square beyond the ideology of division, set a milestone of division literature.

In the industrialization and democratization of the 1970s and 80s, there followed **Hwang Seok-yeong** (〈Samp'o ganeun gil〉, 〈Gaekji〉), who dealt with the alienation of the urban poor and workers; **Jo Se-hui**'s linked-story collection **《Nanjangi-ga sworaollin jageun gong》** (The Little Ball Launched by a Dwarf; denouncing the violence of redevelopment and labor exploitation in a fantastic, poetic style); and the epic and novella narratives of Yi Mun-gu, Jo Jeong-rae, Park Gyeong-ni (《Toji》), Yi Cheong-jun, Kim Won-il, and others, which traced the historical roots of division through shamanism, class, and family history, completing the depth of Korean fiction.

examples.title: Comparing the irony of Hyeon Jin-geon's 〈Unsu joeun nal〉 and Chae Man-sik's 《Taepyeongcheonha》
body: Condition: compare the ways irony is used in Hyeon Jin-geon's 〈Unsu joeun nal〉 (A Lucky Day) of the 1920s and Chae Man-sik's 《Taepyeongcheonha》 (Peace Under Heaven) of the 1930s.

Step 1: 〈Unsu joeun nal〉 maximizes the misery of the colonial lower class through the **situational irony** that a 'lucky day,' unusually profitable for the rickshaw man Kim Cheomji, is in fact 'the most tragic day,' when his sick wife breathes her last at home.

Step 2: In 《Taepyeongcheonha》, a narrator in the manner of pansori lyrics intervenes directly and mocks old Yun Jik-won, who praises colonial reality as 'peace under heaven' because he can keep his property thanks to the Japanese maintenance of order, employing **narrative irony and satire**.
Interpretation: Both works make 'the exact opposite contrast between title and actual reality (irony)' their core device, but the former draws out tragic pity and the latter comic satire.

examples.title: Modernist techniques in Park Tae-won's 〈Soseolga Gubossi-ui ilil〉 and Yi Sang's 〈Nalgae〉
body: Condition: compare the narrative techniques of two modernist novels set in 1930s Gyeongseong (Seoul).

Step 1: 〈Soseolga Gubossi-ui ilil〉 (A Day in the Life of the Novelist Mr. Gubo) combines a **journey structure and inner monologue**, following in long, comma-laden sentences the manners and customs (modernology) and the associations that the novelist Gubo sees and hears as he leaves home and wanders the streets, teahouses, and station of Gyeongseong.

Step 2: 〈Nalgae〉 (Wings) extremely showed the alienation and fragmentation of the modern subject through the fragmented psychology of the protagonist 'I,' a 'genius turned into a stuffed specimen' in a small room cut off from the outer society, and the **stream-of-consciousness** technique in which temporal order is dismantled.
Interpretation: The modernist novel dismantled the causal plot of external events and raised the inner consciousness of the character and the sensations of urban space to the front of the narrative.
