kl-18.title: The Four Coordinates of Literary Criticism and Modern Critical Theories
explain: The discipline that systematizes how to interpret and evaluate literary works is **literary critical theory**. The American critic M. H. Abrams, in *The Mirror and the Lamp*, clearly organized the perspectives of criticism into four coordinates, based on the four elements that make up literary activity: the **work**, the **universe** (the world), the **artist** (the author), and the **audience** (the reader).

These four coordinates divide in turn into three **extrinsic perspectives**, which connect the work with the external contexts surrounding it, and one **intrinsic perspective**, which concentrates only on the linguistic structure inside the work. The extrinsic perspectives are: (1) the **mimetic theory** (반영론; world-centered), which looks at how the work reflects the historical and social reality of its time; (2) the **expressive theory** (표현론; author-centered), which looks at how the work expresses the author's inner feelings, biographical experience, and creative intention; and (3) the **pragmatic theory** (효용론; reader-centered), which looks at what lesson, pleasure, or change of perception the work gives its readers.

explain.alt: A diagram of Abrams's four-coordinate system of literary criticism. Centered on the work in the middle (objective theory, the intrinsic perspective), the universe above (mimetic theory), the author on the left (expressive theory), and the reader on the right (pragmatic theory) are connected to it.
explain.caption: Intrinsic criticism analyzes the linguistic form of the work itself; extrinsic criticism analyzes its relation to the world, the author, and the reader.

explain: By contrast, the **intrinsic perspective (objective theory, structural theory)** puts in brackets such external information as the author's biography, the historical background, and the reader's impressions, and precisely analyzes only the **linguistic order inside the text**. Representative intrinsic criticisms are Russian **Formalism** in the first half of the 20th century (Shklovsky's **'defamiliarization'**, which twists everyday language to renew perception), Anglo-American **New Criticism** (which rejects the intentional fallacy and the affective fallacy and performs a **close reading** of paradox, irony, tension, and organic unity), and French **Structuralism** (which, based on Saussurean linguistics, analyzes narrative grammar and binary-opposition structures).

From the late 20th century on, critical theory absorbed the achievements of intrinsic analysis while again going beyond the closed boundary of the text. The **historical and sociological criticism** of Lukács and Goldmann refined the mimetic theory, and the **reception aesthetics (reader-response criticism)** of Jauss and Iser accomplished a modern turn of the pragmatic theory, holding that the reader completes meaning by filling the 'gaps' of the text. Furthermore, **post-structuralism (deconstruction)** exposed the instability of binary oppositions within the text, and **feminist, postcolonial, and ecocritical criticism** critically decode the power structures of gender, imperialism, and the exploitation of nature hidden within literary texts.

examples.title: Reading one poem (Yun Dong-ju's 〈Seosi〉) with the four critical coordinates
body: Condition: apply each of Abrams's four coordinates to Yun Dong-ju's poem 〈Seosi〉 (Prologue) (`죽는 날까지 하늘을 우러러 한 점 부끄럼이 없기를...`, 'May I, until the day I die, look up to heaven with not a speck of shame...').

Step 1: The **expressive theory** reads the Christian conscience of the poet Yun Dong-ju and the anguish of his student days abroad; the **mimetic theory** reads the historical oppression of the colonial dark period at the end of Japanese rule in the 1940s; and the **pragmatic theory** analyzes the moral reflection and emotion that today's readers gain from reading this poem.

Step 2: The **intrinsic (objective) perspective**, setting aside Yun Dong-ju's life and the background knowledge of the Japanese colonial period, precisely analyzes only the opposition of images between `'하늘·별·바람'` ('sky, stars, wind') and `'잎새·밤'` ('leaves, night') inside the poem, and the arrangement of tenses and the tone: past (`괴로워했다`, 'I suffered'), future (`사랑해야지`, 'I must love'), and present (`스치운다`, 'it brushes by').
Interpretation: The four perspectives are not rival claims to a single right answer, but complementary lenses that illuminate in three dimensions the multilayered meanings held by a single text.

examples.title: Russian Formalism's 'defamiliarization' and New Criticism's 'two fallacies'
body: Condition: examine two core concepts of intrinsic criticism: Shklovsky's 'defamiliarization' and New Criticism's 'intentional fallacy and affective fallacy'.

Step 1: **Defamiliarization** is the technique of transforming things or language that have become automatic in daily life and are passed over numbly into something strange and rough, thereby prolonging the reader's time of perception, and the Formalists saw the essence of 'literariness' in this.

Step 2: The Anglo-American New Critics (Wimsatt and Beardsley) called the attitude of seeking a work's meaning in the author's creative intention the **intentional fallacy**, and the attitude of reducing it to the reader's subjective psychological response the **affective fallacy**, and argued for the close reading of the text itself.

Interpretation: Formalism and New Criticism contributed greatly to freeing literary study from being a handmaid of history or psychology and establishing it as an independent science of text analysis.

kl-19.title: Bachelor's Capstone I: Grammatical and Phonological Analysis and Cross-Period Reading of Texts
explain: The first step in synthesizing the bachelor's course in Korean language and literature is to apply the precise analytical tools of **Korean linguistics (phonology, morphology, syntax, and the history of the language)** to the actual sentences of **Korean literature (classical and modern poetry and narrative texts)** and to read across them. This is because a literary work is not an idea in a vacuum but a language art shaped by the phonological system, the rules of morpheme combination, the sentence structure, and the honorific and pragmatic tone of a particular period.

In reading classical texts, **Middle and Early Modern Korean grammar** and **classical metrics** work at the same time. For example, when decoding 15th-century documents or classical poetry, restoring continuous writing (이어적기; `기퍼 → 깊어`) to separated writing, and grasping the old phonemes (`ㆍ, ㅸ, ㅿ`), tones and vowel harmony, and the combinatory principle of the object-honorific pre-final ending (`-삽-`) and the nominative particle (`이/ㅣ`), reveals the exact contextual meaning of the text. Layering on top of this a reading by the 3-foot meter (Goryeo songs and folk songs), the 4-foot meter (sijo and gasa), and the rule that fixes the first foot of the final verse at three syllables makes the poetic rhythm and the turning point of the poetic thought clear.

In analyzing modern literary texts too, **morphology, syntax, and pragmatics** provide decisive clues. Analyzing why a poet coined an unfamiliar non-syntactic compound or derived word instead of a syntactic compound (Formalism's 'defamiliarization'), why a novelist used a long sentence with adnominal, noun, and adverbial clauses embedded layer upon layer (an embedding sentence) instead of a short simple sentence to delay a character's fragmented inner life (stream of consciousness), or why dialogue employs ironic indirect speech acts and asymmetric honorifics instead of direct speech acts objectively proves the aesthetic effect of the style.

When the **microscopic analysis of linguistic form** (Korean linguistics) is thus combined with the **macroscopic context of genre, period, and ideology** (literary history and criticism), empirical textual criticism at the bachelor's level, going beyond impressionistic appreciation, is completed.

examples.title: Integrated reading of a classical poem line by the history of the language and meter
body: Condition: simultaneously analyze the pyeongsijo final verse `'각시님 달이야카니와 궂은비나 되쇼셔'` ('Dear lady, not to say the moon, may you be at least the dreary rain'; the same structure as the closing phrase of Jeong Cheol's 〈Samiingok〉) by Korean grammar and poetic meter.

Step 1 (metrical analysis): It is read in breaks as `'각시님(3) / 달이야카니와(6) / 궂은비나(4) / 되쇼셔(3)'`, and exactly meets the rule of the sijo final verse and the closing of regular gasa: the first foot fixed at three syllables and the second foot of five syllables or more.

Step 2 (morphology and honorific analysis): `'궂은비'` is a **syntactic compound** in which the adnominal ending `'-은'` and the noun `'비'` are attached to the predicate stem `'궂-'`, and `'되쇼셔'` is a Middle and Early Modern Korean addressee-honorific imperative sentence-final ending that elevates the beloved (the addressee) with the highest honorific.
Interpretation: The meter (3·6·4·3), the word formation (syntactic compound), and the addressee honorifics combine to complete the tone of earnest longing toward the beloved.

examples.title: Analysis of the syntactic structure and irony of a modern novel sentence
body: Condition: analyze a hypothetical sentence `'그날 그가 집을 나섰을 때, 아내가 다시는 눈을 뜨지 못하리라는 사실을 그는 끝내 알지 못했다'` ('The day he left the house, he never knew the fact that his wife would never open her eyes again') by syntax and narratology.

Step 1 (syntactic analysis): The whole sentence is a multiple **embedding sentence** (complex sentence) that holds an adverbial clause (`그날 그가 집을 나섰을 때`, 'the day he left the house') and an appositive adnominal clause (`[아내가 다시는 눈을 뜨지 못하리라는] 사실`, 'the fact that his wife would never open her eyes again'), and the main predicate `'알다'` ('know') is a two-place predicate requiring a subject (`그는`) and an object (`사실을`).

Step 2 (narrative and critical analysis): By having the omniscient narrator present in advance, in an appositive adnominal clause, the tragic future the character (`그`, 'he') does not know (`아내의 죽음`, 'his wife's death'), the sentence forms **tragic irony** through the information gap between reader and character.

Interpretation: The syntactic embedding structure of the appositive adnominal clause functions as a grammatical device that realizes the foreshadowing of the omniscient point of view and situational irony.

kl-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone II: Analysis of Linguistic Form and Designing a Pluralist Critical Essay
explain: The final capstone task of the bachelor's course in Korean language and literature is to choose one literary text (from classical poetry, pansori and the classical novel, modern poetry, and the modern novel) and to design and write a complete **integrated critical essay** that combines **linguistic analysis of form from Korean linguistics** with **literary critical theory (intrinsic and extrinsic perspectives)**.

A persuasive critical essay in Korean language and literature consists of the following five stages. **(1) Target text and statement of the problem**: select the work (or genre) to be analyzed and pose a core question that goes beyond received opinion. **(2) Microscopic analysis of linguistic form (tools of Korean linguistics)**: present, with concrete textual evidence, the phonology and meter used in the work (3-foot or 4-foot, phonological alternation), vocabulary and morphology (derived and compound words, the opposition of native and Sino-Korean words), and syntactic and pragmatic structures (embedding sentences, honorifics, indirect speech acts and irony).

**(3) Intrinsic criticism (analysis of structure and aesthetics)**: explain how the linguistic forms analyzed above create paradox, irony, defamiliarization, and narrative tension (a dream-framed structure, a hero's life story, stream of consciousness, etc.) inside the work. **(4) Extrinsic criticism (the context of period, author, and reader)**: connect the internal structure of the text, in three dimensions, to the historical and social reality of its time (mimetic theory: the shaking of the status system in late Joseon, the period of Japanese rule, division and industrialization, etc.), to the orientation of the author's consciousness (expressive theory), and to the reader's mode of reception (pragmatic theory).

**(5) Critical synthesis and reflection on limits**: conclude by showing how the essay has balanced the historicity that is easily missed when one stays with intrinsic analysis alone, and the literary autonomy (the distinctiveness of a language art) that is easily damaged when one leans only toward extrinsic mimetic theory. This task is not automatically scored; through the checklist you yourself check whether your critical essay has the argumentation and empirical grounds of the bachelor's level.

examples.title: Example design of an integrated critical essay (topic: the late Joseon pansori-based novel 〈Chunhyangjeon〉)
body: Step 1 (linguistic form and intrinsic analysis): Analyze the 4-foot verse-like style of 〈Chunhyangjeon〉, the expansive style of enumeration and parallelism, and the dual-language structure in which yangban Chinese-style vocabulary and commoner vulgar words and humor collide within a single sentence.

Step 2 (extrinsic and social-historical analysis): Argue that this linguistic duality arises from the social-historical position of the pansori gwangdae (mimetic and pragmatic theories), who in the shaking of the status system and the development of commerce in late Joseon had to receive both a yangban audience (the surface theme of the Confucian virtuous woman) and a commoner audience (the underlying theme of liberation from status and criticism of corrupt officials).

Interpretation: The microscopic features of style and vocabulary (Korean linguistics) and the duality of theme and social-historical context (literary studies) are integrated into one coherent thesis.

examples.title: Example design of an integrated critical essay (topic: the 1930s modernist novel and the embedding-sentence style)
body: Step 1 (linguistic form and intrinsic analysis): Syntactically analyze how the long embedding sentences joined by commas in the novels of Park Tae-won or Yi Sang (multiple embedding of adnominal and noun clauses) and the frequent use of present-tense endings slow the pace of events and realize 'stream of consciousness'.

Step 2 (extrinsic and literary-historical analysis): Show that this syntactic delay and fragmented inner monologue are the formal counterpart that most honestly reveals the modernization of colonial Gyeongseong in the 1930s and the alienation of intellectuals with no way out (mimetic and expressive theories).
Interpretation: One can demonstrate that grammatical syntactic structure is itself an aesthetic form reflecting the inner life of an era.
